sentences.text: Brachauchenius was an extinct genus of pliosaurs characterized by a large, elongated skull and a short neck, a body plan typical of thalassophonean pliosaurids.
The holotype specimen is estimated to have reached a maximum length of 5.3 meters and a body mass of 2.2 tons, though other sources suggest the animal grew to nearly 10 meters in total length.
The genus name Brachauchenius means "short neck" in Ancient Greek and Latin, a name chosen because the original skeleton was believed to possess the shortest neck of any described plesiosaur.
This genus represents the last appearance of a pliosaur in North America, marking the end of this group's presence on the continent.
The first known specimen, cataloged as USNM 4989, was collected by Charles H. Sternberg in Ottawa County, Kansas, in 1884, shortly after a quarry owner near Delphos discovered the holotype skeleton.
Samuel Wendell Williston formally named the fossil Brachauchenius lucasi in 1903 based on these early finds.
Additional specimens were found later, including one from Morocco that was officially assigned to the species in 2016.

A Fairport skull was officially described as the new genus Megacephalosaurus eulerti in 2013 by Schumacher, Carpenter, and Everhart, following its discovery in 1950 by brothers Frank and Robert Jennrich.
Photos found in 2007 revealed that the Fairport skull had underside features distinct from other Brachauchenius lucasi skulls.

A larger specimen, FHSM VP-321, with a cranial length of 170 centimeters, was excavated by George F. Sternberg in 1952 from the Fairport Limestone in Russell County, Kansas, and later described by Carpenter.
The specimen FHSM VP-321 was later assigned to its own genus and species, Megacephalosaurus eulerti.

A skeleton initially described as Brachauchenius in 2005 was reclassified as the new genus Stenorhynchosaurus munozi in 2016 after being discovered in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, in 2000 and exhumed between 2004 and 2005.
Microscopic analysis in 2005 dated the holotype to the early Middle Turonian based on its origin in the Greenhorn Limestone or Fairport Chalk.
Brachauchenius belongs to the family Pliosauridae and is classified within the subfamily Brachaucheninae.
Brachauchenius lived during the Late Cretaceous in regions that are now North America and North Africa.
The type species, Brachauchenius lucasi, lived in the western interior sea of North America between 93.5 and 89.3 million years ago during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
The genus lived from the Barremian to the Turonian, spanning from 125.77 to 89.8 million years ago.

It is debated whether some specimens currently attributed to Brachauchenius actually belong to the genus Megacephalosaurus, as later analyses showed that a Colombian specimen referred to Brachauchenius was distinct enough to warrant a new genus and species, named Stenorhynchosaurus munozi.
